name: DART (Double Asteroid Redirection Test)
significance: DART was launched to provide the first real-world test of whether deliberately crashing a spacecraft into an asteroid could measurably change its orbit, a foundational question for planetary defense against a future hazardous impactor. It was the first mission in history to intentionally alter the motion of a celestial body, targeting the small moonlet Dimorphos in the Didymos binary system as a proxy for the size of asteroid most likely to threaten Earth. The kinetic impact on 26 September 2022 shortened Dimorphos's 11.9-hour orbital period by about 33 minutes, far exceeding the 73-second threshold considered a success, because ejecta recoil amplified the momentum transfer by a factor of roughly three to four beyond the spacecraft's own momentum. Follow-up analysis showed Dimorphos to be a weak, cohesionless rubble pile that was measurably reshaped and had its orbit altered by the collision, validating kinetic impact as a viable planetary defense technique.
statusNote: First full-scale planetary-defense kinetic-impact test. Direct Earth-to-Didymos transfer, no flyby waypoints -- the simplest architecture in this catalog's asteroid-mission batch. Deliberately impacted Dimorphos (Didymos's small moon, not modeled separately -- see SMALL_BODIES comment in app.js) on 2022-09-26 at ~6.1 km/s, shortening its orbital period around Didymos by 32 minutes and proving kinetic deflection works. Spacecraft destroyed on impact; the DRACO imager kept transmitting until the moment of collision.
